text: The assembly will now hear an address by
his excellency John Ramani Mahama,
President of the Republic of Ghana. I
request
I request protocol to escort his
excellency and invite him to address the
assembly.
Mr. President,
Mr. Secretary General, your
excellencies,
distinguished delegates, ladies and
gentlemen,
let me congratulate you, Mr. president
on your election to preside over the
81st session of the United Nations
General Assembly.
You assume this solemn stewardship at a
time of intense geopolitical
fragmentation,
deepening inequality and eroded trust in
our multilateral system.
Ghana is confident that your proven
commitment to inclusive, consultative
and principled dialogue will guide this
assembly well and you have our full
support.
I also wish to commend outgoing UN
Secretary General Antonio Guterres for
his dedicated service to our world body
over the last 10 years.
Mr. President,
Ghana's national anthem contains a
profound petition. It asked God to make
us bold to defend forever the cause of
freedom and of right. And those words
gave my compatriots and I courage to
uphold the Panaffrican and anticolonial
heritage that was bequipped to us by our
forbears.
Another line in our item petitions God
to fill our hearts with true humility
and make us cherish fearless honesty.
That prayer inspires me today to follow
in the footsteps of Drwa Kruma, Hill
Salassie, Nelson Mandela and other
global icons who have stood at this very
podium before me and have spoken boldly
and fearlessly about the state of
affairs in our world.
The words the world may not transform
overnight because of the speeches that
we deliver here in this August assembly,
but history would faithfully record the
truths we choose to speak and the
silences that we choose to keep when
we're granted the privilege of
addressing this global town hall.
Allow me therefore to begin by
reintroducing myself to the general
assembly. I stand before you as
president of the Republic of Ghana. Yet
we too often ascend these heights draped
only in the ropes of our titles,
forgetting that alongside each of us
stands a history, a people, and a
legacy.
I was born in a little town, Damangu,
which was then a modest community in
northern Ghana and is now the capital of
the Savana region of my country. I was
born to Mr. Emmanuel Adama Mahama of Ble
and Madame Abiba Naba of Bunu both of
blessed memory.
I belong to them and I belong to the
four mothers and the forefathers who
gave birth to them, who named them, who
nurtured them and who passed down the
enduring values by which I live today.
I grew up at the crossroads of several
Ghanaian cultures. I speak Gongja which
is a Guan language. I speak tree and
Ghan. I am fluent in Hower spoken across
the West African savannah in the Sahil.
I understand somewhere
and I speak English as my official
language. In a very real sense, I belong
to all these people because their
tongues including English have become my
tongue. Language creates a kingship
regardless of the historical
complexities through which kinship was
forged. Mr. President,
everybody in this chamber today and
every global citizen listening to my
words possesses an origin. We carry
inherited memories, values, rich
cultures, and distinct identities of our
homelands.
Belonging anchors us and it reminds us
that we are part of a human story that
is far larger than ourselves.
It is a vital wellspring of dignity and
pride. But belonging also has its dark
side. When belonging is weaponized by
political expediency, it transforms into
native nativism, chauvinism, xenophobia,
and the dangerous prejudices that are
extended to people who are deemed
different from us. It becomes the
pretext for discrimination, for
displacement, for persecution and war.
And yet for this organization, the
United Nations, the founding principles
remain immutable.
Every human being belongs to the human
family.
No race is superior. No nation is
inferior. No child,
no child's life is worthless because of
the language they speak or the faith
they profess or the color of their skin
or the land of their birth. This is the
unyielding moral foundation upon which
the United Nations must stand. I'll
return to this issue of belonging at the
end of my speech. But Mr. President,
last year from this very podium, I made
a solemn pledge on behalf of Africa and
the global African diaspora to seek full
international recognition of the
transatlantic trafficking and racialized
chat, enslavement of Africans as the
gravest crime against humanity.
Some cautioned that we were reopening
old wounds. But we came not to provoke
division or render empty judgment. We
came to seek healing. And true healing
requires truth. And truth requires
acknowledgements. And acknowledgement
must lead to meaningful repair.
Mr. President, for centuries, this
tragedy was rendered in the passive
voice as though the millions of African
men, women, and children just vanished
into the shadows of time. Mr. President,
they do not v vanish. They were hunted.
They were captured. They were
trafficked. They were bought. They were
sold. They were exploited and exchanged
for profit. They were ripped from their
families and communities they belong to.
Their unpaid labor built the cities,
industries, banking institutions, and
empires of the modern western world.
Meanwhile, the African continent was
left depopulated,
split families, structural disruption,
and generational trauma. Mr. President,
on 25th March this year, the
international day of remembrance of the
victims of slavery and the transatlantic
slave trade, Ghana had the honor of
tableabling resolution 80/250
in this very August assembly. Mr.
President,
123 nations voted to affirm this
fundamental truth that the transatlantic
slave trade and charter enslavement were
the gravest crimes against humanity.
I stand with respect at this p p p p p p
p p p p p p p p p p p p p p p p p p p p
p p p p p p p p p p p p p p podium to
thank every nation that voted for
justice and I'm deeply grateful to our
brothers and sisters in the African
Union, the CARICOM, Celac and our
partners across the global south. That
resolution was not a mere gesture. It
was adopted because the structural
legacies of those historic crimes
continue to fuel systematic racism,
economic marginalization, and a global
financial architecture that is weighted
against Africa and people of African
descent.
Since the passage of the historic
resolution, we welcome the positive
overtures from many countries and
institutions that have joined the
dialogue on reparative justice. The
Netherlands, Germany, and France have
all made positive moves to join the
conversation on reparatory justice. Mr.
President, real repair demands
structural transformation. It requires
dismantling the persistent engines of
exploitation, unfair global trade,
predatory resource extraction,
discriminated discriminatory credit
ratings, unsustainable debt burdens of
the global south, and the continued
export of raw materials from Africa
while real value addition and job
creation occur elsewhere.
Mr. President, the injustices of the
past remain embedded in today's power
structures.
Africa is home to 1.5 billion people,
over 18% of humanity, and constitutes
the largest regional voting block in
this general assembly. And yet, Africa
rem remains without a single permanent
seat on the United Nations Security
Council. This is fundamentally
unacceptable in the 21st century.
Africa must be granted permanent
representation on the UN Security
Council complete with all the rights and
responsibilities.
We cannot credibly champion the
sovereign equality of nations while
preserving a global governance structure
that was designed for the post-war
geopolitical realities.
Mr. President, Security Council reform
is not a favor to Africa. It is an
imperative for the legitimacy, the
credibility and the survival of the
United Nations.
The same systemic inequalities permeates
the international financial
architecture.
Developing nations and the global south
borrow at interest rates that are up to
eight times higher than industrialized
nations.
African and Caribbean nations struck by
climate disasters are forced to take on
crippling debts to rebuild from floods
and droughts that they did not cause.
Governments are forced into a tragic
choice to service predatory debt or to
serve their people.
We demand reform. We need long-term
affordable and accessible concessionary
financing that enables developing
economies to invest in human capital in
industrialization and climate
adaptation.
Mr. President, Africa does not seek
charity. Africa seeks equal partnership
that is anchored
that is anchored in mutual respect. Our
continent possesses the world's youngest
population, vast arable lands,
unparalleled cultural vitality, and the
critical minerals required to drive the
global green energy transition. But, Mr.
Speaker,
let me warn Africa will not remain a
passive arena for a new scramble for
resources.
Critical mineral extraction in Africa
must not replicate the colonial era
exploitation.
We will process our minerals at home.
We will build local industries that
create dignified jobs for our youth and
we retain the value of our natural
resources in Africa.
The African continental free trade area
whose secretariat Ghana is proud to host
is our engine for intra African trade
structural transformation and industrial
growth. As we heal historical wounds, we
must address the alarming breakdown of
the current global order. We are
witnessing a dangerous shift towards
unilateralism, lawlessness, and the
erosion of multilateral norms. The
United Nations must learn from the
lessons of the League of Nations.
The UN Charter must reign supreme over
the cynical doctrine that might makes
right.
The veto power must never serve as a
license for impunity.
Sovereign equality cannot be a private
privilege that is reserved only for
nations that are aligned with global
superpowers.
And nowhere is this crisis of
credibility more painful than in the
ongoing persecution of the Palestinian
people in Gaza and the West Bank.
Mr. Speaker, Mr. President, sorry I was
an MP before. Mr. President, the time
has come for us to stop using diplomatic
euphemisms to ve the human carnage that
is taking place in Gaza. How many more
lives must be lost before the world acts
with decisive moral author authority?
The blood of 5-year-old Hind Rajab and
the more than 20,000 children that have
been killed in this brutal conflict
cries out to the conscience of the
world.
Collective punishment and forced
starvation and mass displacement are
flagrant violations of international
law.
Ghana remains unwavering in its
recognition of the sovereign state of
Palestine and its steadfast support for
a viable two-state solution where Israel
and Palestine will live side by side in
peace, security with guaranteed borders.
At the same time, we condemn all acts of
terrorism by Hamas that triggered this
conflict and we insist that all parties
unconditionally respect international
humanitarian law. Our moral standards
cannot be selective.
In that spirit of international
legality, in that same spirit
international legality and human
solidarity, Ghana reiterates its call
for the immediate lifting of the
decadesl long economic, commercial, and
financial embargo that has been imposed
on Cuba.
The world must support Cuba's new
economic and social program. Measures
that inflict collective economic
hardship on ordinary citizens run
counter to our shared commitment to
human dignity and international law. We
must likewise elevate our global
response to the catastrophic conflict in
Sudan, which is reported to be the
world's worst humanitarian crisis. We
must also ex exercise solidarity with
nations that are facing the ter
terrorist scorge especially our
neighbors in the alliance of Sahel
states.
The current Middle East crisis is having
a deliterous effect on the world
economy. We call for a return to the
negotiating table and let me add that no
human civilization deserves to be
annihilated and certainly not a member
of the United Nations.
I believe that dialogue can resolve even
the most intractable of global problems
across every conflict whether in Europe,
the Middle East, Africa. The standard
must remain uniform, respect for
sovereign integrity, protect civilians,
ensure unhindered humanitarian access
and hold perpetrators of war crimes
accountable.
Mr. President, those who have declared
climate change a hoax perpetrated by
geopolitical opponents,
the warnings of recent times cannot have
been clearer.
melting glaciers, flash flood, flooding,
droughts, record-breaking heat waves,
brush fires, hurricanes, and other
extreme weather phenomena are
unmistakable signs of an overburdened
planet.
Climate change is the ultimate test of
global equity.
We in Africa contribute less than 4% of
global greenhouse gases and yet we bear
some of the heaviest burden of climate
devastation.
We face erratic rainfall. Our coastal
towns suffer relentless erosion. And our
Sahilian region faces accelerating
desertification.
On 29th June this year, Ghana and
coastal West Africa faced an
unprecedented deluge.
Torrential rain exceeding 160 mm was
dumped on seven coastal regions of Ghana
within 24 hours, resulting in 39 deaths
and one still unaccounted for. And so
climate justice demands that developed
nations must fulfill their long overdue
financial commitments. Mitigation
support must be operationalized with
predictable non-debt creating grants,
not loans that further in debt fragile
economies.
Similarly, global health security
demands true solidarity because
pathogens do not respect national
borders. They just walk across without
visas.
We must build an equitable global health
architecture that guarantees regional
manufacturing of vaccines and
therapeutics, strengthen epidemic
surveillance and funds resilient public
health infrastructure across the global
south in accordance with the demands of
the Ara reset.
Mr. President, excellencies, I agree
that even as we demand a place at the
table and call for a more equitable and
just global order as African leaders, we
must also do what is required to put our
own houses in order.
As the legal maxim goes, whoever comes
into equity must come with clean hands.
African leadership must be transparent
and accountable. We must commit to the
fight against corruption and ensure that
every dollar of our people's money
counts and is used efficiently in their
interest.
Ghana is arguably the most stable
democracy in Africa. We believe in the
rule of law and have respect for human
rights and we're determined to
demonstrate that democracy works.
While progress in a democracy may be
slow because it must follow
constitutional processes, it is more
sustainable because it is built through
popular participation and consensus
building.
As Ghana addresses these global
imperatives, we are leading by example
at home through our transformative
resetting Ghana agenda.
Less than two years into my
administration, through disciplined
governance and fiscal prudence and an
uncompromising fight against corruption,
Ghana has achieved a dramatic economic
turnaround.
Indeed, some circles describe it as a
Ghanaian miracle.
Our macroeconomic stabilization measures
have restored growth, drastically
reduced inflation, stabilized our
national currency, and significantly
lowered our public debt burden. This
remarkable economic recover recovery
story has been independently validated
by all the multilateral financial
institutions and major international
credit rating agencies all of which
affirm that Ghana has moved from
economic vulnerability to sustained
recovery, resilience and growth.
But Mr. President, macroeconomic
indicators mean little if they do not
translate into real improvements in our
people's daily lives. Economic growth
and progress must have a human face. And
that is why we're pursuing an aggressive
national infrastructure agenda under our
big push program to build roads, expand
digital connectivity, construct schools
and health facilities.
This strategic investment is opening up
the length and breadth of our country,
bridging the rural urban divide,
unlocking agricultural potential, and
guaranteeing equipable access to basic
services for every Ghanaian, no matter
where they live in our country.
Through our flagship 24-hour economy and
accelerated exports development program
and the soontobe launched new Ghana e
economy policy, we're transforming Ghana
into an industrial high productivity
hub. We're incentivizing roundthe-clock
commercial operations, driving value
addition in agriculture, mining, and
creating sustainable dignified jobs for
our vibrant youth and women. And central
to our national reset is a revolutionary
expansion of social protection,
universal healthcare, delivering on the
sustainable development goals,
specifically SDG1 on poverty, SDG3 on
good health and well-being, and SDG10 on
reduced inequalities. And so Ghana has
officially launched a historic free
primary health care program ensuring
that every Gandhian can access essential
primary health care services at their
community level at zero cost.
This program has been hailed by the
World Health Organization and the United
Nations as a benchmark paradigm shift
for the global south and this model is
currently being studied by other nations
that are seeking to achieve true
universal health coverage.
Alongside our national health insurance
scheme, we've introduced a specialized
fund officially named Ghana Medical
Trust Fund, but popularly referred to
after my name, Mahhamare,
that guarantees Ghanaians suffering from
non-communicable diseases such as renal
failure, cancers, cardiovascular
diseases, and diabetes. It guarantees
that they receive subsidized,
affordable, and life-saving care.
I've always believed that democracy must
deliver tangible social benefits.
Citizens must experience democracy not
only through the ballot box every four
years, but through improved access to
food, quality education, decent housing,
accessible health care, and economic
opportunities.
Mr. President, democracy loses its soul
when it protects elite privileges while
abandoning the vulnerable.
And so Ghana remains an uncompromising
beacon of constitutional democracy,
medium of freedom, the rule of law, and
peaceful transitions of power on the
African continent.
But these domestic achievements set the
stage for two historic milestones ahead
of us. In March 2027,
Ghana will celebrate its 70th
anniversary of independence as the first
nation in subsaharan Africa to break the
shackles of colonial domination.
And in January 2027, Ghana will proudly
assume the chairmanship of the African
Union.
I wish to serve notice that we intend to
use our AU chairmanship to champion
continental integration, accelerate the
implementation of the African
continental free trade area, push for
peace and security in all the conflict
zones of Africa, and ensure that Africa
speaks on the global stage with one
resolute, undivided and confident voice.
Mr. President, the doubting crisis
confronting our world are not
insurmountable. What we lack is not
resources or intellect. What we lack is
the political courage to see one another
as a part of a single human family.
We must see each other not as strategic
rivals, economic targets or demographic
threats, but as human beings who belong.
That refugee fleeing violence belongs.
That migrant seeking opportunity
belongs.
That child in Gaza, Sudan or Ukraine
belongs.
The descendants of enslaved Africans
seeking justice belong. The indigenous
community protecting its ancestral lands
and environment belongs.
The small island state threatened by
rising oceans belong to humanity. The
poor, the vulnerable and the
marginalized belong.
They belong to our common human family.
And because they belong, we must
safeguard their dignity. We must enforce
their rights. And most of all, we must
hear their voices. When our first
president of Sajifu, Dr. Awami Kuma
stood on the eve of our independence in
1957. He declared that the independence
of Ghana is meaningless unless it is
linked up with the total liberation of
the African continent.
Today, from this respected global
podium, we must expand that historic
truth. The freedom of any nation is
insecure unless it is linked to the
freedom of all humanity.
In Ghana, we believe that our national
prosperity is fragile unless it is a
shared prosperity.
Our global peace is unviable unless it
is anchored in justice.
Let this general assembly recommit
itself to a world where belonging is
used not to erect walls but to build
bridges, not to exclude, but to unite,
not to degrade humanity, but to exalt.
Let us speak truth with humility.
Let us act with courage. And as I said
from the Gand National Anthem, let us
cherish fearless honesty in the
statements that we deliver today at this
podium and in the choices we make
tomorrow. May God bless our shared
world. May God bless my homeland, Ghana.
And may God bless the United Nations. I
thank you.
On behalf of the assembly,
I wish to thank the President of the
Republic of Ghana.
